svg.title: How extensive is an exceedance?
svg.desc: Infographic in four panels on how an exceedance of an air quality standard is quantified. 1: what is computed, with an invented example: surface, people, roads, vegetation. 2: the five steps: exceedance area, surface, people, roads, vegetation. 3: the sources of uncertainty: resolution of the population map, residents or people present, road network considered. 4: which model to use and what to document.
svg.text: How an exceedance is quantified · Commission technical support document (April 2025), §3.5 · Dir. (EU) 2024/2881

text.tspan: invented example: the red area exceeds the
NO2 limit set to protect health

g.text: of the area above the standard

text.tspan: living in the area (if the
standard protects health)
of roads above the standard (if
traffic is the cause)
km² of sensitive vegetation (if
the standard protects it)
From the model map (reference year) take the
zones above the standard (limit value, target
value or critical level), without places where
compliance is not assessed, such as the
carriageway.
Overlay the map of residents on the area and add
up the inhabitants.
In street canyons in exceedance, add up the
length of the segments: a road is one segment,
however many lanes it has.
Overlay the map of sensitive vegetation and
compute the km² inside the area. Exclude areas
within 20 km of cities, or within 5 km of other
built-up zones, industry and roads with over 50
000 vehicles a day, except vulnerable areas.
Cells of 0.5 km² or smaller: with larger
cells those exposed are underestimated.
In canyons the buildings facing the
street count.
Residents are counted, not the whole
zone. In city centres many people work,
study or seek care without living there:
residents may underestimate those
exposed.
The total depends on the roads
considered: a complete, declared network
is best. For open roads use the surface.
same city, different network: very different totals
(sketch)
One that meets at least the
modelling quality objective (MQO).
Where concentrations change a lot
from point to point, the model
must reproduce these gradients.
For traffic hotspots, use street
canyon models (narrow streets
between buildings).
Method and results described in
the plan, for transparency and
comparability (Annex V, point E).

g.text: Quantifying an exceedance: the surface, people, roads and vegetation exposed depend heavily on method and input data.
That is why fit-for-purpose models and a documented, transparent methodology are needed.
